lesson.title: Brain Imaging Methods: Tools for Watching a Living Mind
lesson.summary: Modern brain imaging techniques let psychologists apply the scientific method directly to the central nervous system, revealing brain structure and activity with varying degrees of precision in space and time.
lesson.body:
For most of the history of psychology, understanding how the central nervous system produced thought, emotion, and behavior depended almost entirely on studying patients with brain damage after the fact, comparing what a person could no longer do with the location of an injury discovered only through autopsy. Applying the scientific method to the living, functioning brain required new tools capable of measuring structure and activity safely, precisely, and repeatably in people who were very much alive. Several distinct imaging technologies now make this possible, and each offers a different tradeoff between spatial resolution, or how precisely a technique can pinpoint location, and temporal resolution, or how precisely it can track changes over time.

Electroencephalography, or EEG, is one of the oldest and still widely used methods. Electrodes placed on the scalp detect tiny electrical voltage changes produced by the combined activity of large populations of neurons firing together beneath them. EEG offers excellent temporal resolution, capturing changes in brain activity within milliseconds, which makes it especially valuable for studying processes that unfold quickly, such as tracking the distinct stages of sleep discussed later in this chapter. Its major limitation is spatial resolution. Because the electrical signal detected at the scalp represents the blurred sum of activity from many neurons across a wide area, EEG cannot pinpoint exactly which small brain structure produced a given signal.

Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, takes a very different approach, using strong magnetic fields and radio waves, rather than radiation, to produce highly detailed structural images of brain anatomy. An MRI scan can reveal the size, shape, and integrity of specific structures, useful for detecting tumors, injuries, or structural abnormalities, but a standard MRI produces a static picture rather than a record of ongoing activity. Functional MRI, or fMRI, builds on the same magnetic technology but tracks something different: changes in blood oxygen levels in different brain regions over time. Because active neurons demand more oxygenated blood, fMRI can indirectly infer which regions are working harder during a particular task, offering good spatial resolution alongside moderate temporal resolution, though with an inherent delay of a few seconds due to how quickly blood flow actually responds to neural activity.

Positron emission tomography, or PET, offers another window into brain function. A small amount of a radioactive tracer, often attached to a sugar molecule the brain uses for fuel, is introduced into the bloodstream, and the scanner detects where that tracer accumulates most heavily, revealing which regions are consuming the most energy at a given moment. PET can measure specific chemical processes, such as levels of particular neurotransmitter receptors, though it involves radiation exposure and is more invasive than EEG or standard MRI.

Together, these methods give psychologists a toolkit for testing hypotheses about brain and behavior with the same rigor the scientific method demands: precise measurement, replicable procedures, and the ability to compare brain activity across different conditions or groups of people. A researcher curious whether the occipital lobe activates more strongly during a visual task than during rest can now test that question directly using fMRI rather than relying solely on inference from rare cases of brain damage, a real shift in how confidently psychology can make claims about the living brain.
